EKS Managed Node Groups vs. EKS Fargate — Compute Plane Strategy

EKS offers two compute plane models: Managed Node Groups (EC2 instances managed by AWS in your account) and EKS Fargate (serverless pods — AWS manages the underlying compute, fully invisible to the customer). Managed Node Groups give full control over instance types, storage, GPU, and networking. Fargate abstracts all node management but adds constraints: no DaemonSets, limited storage options, higher per-vCPU cost, and slower pod startup. The decision depends on workload requirements, team operational model, and cost profile.

Decision rules:
- USE Managed Node Groups as the default compute plane for production EKS — maximum flexibility, supports DaemonSets, GPU, local NVMe, and Spot
- USE EKS Fargate for: batch Jobs and CronJobs that should not consume cluster node capacity, or lightweight workloads where node management overhead is undesirable
- USE EKS Fargate ONLY when: workload has no DaemonSet requirement, uses no hostPath/hostNetwork, and pod startup time of 60-90 seconds is acceptable
- AVOID Fargate for: latency-sensitive APIs (slower cold start), GPU workloads, DaemonSet-based logging agents, and stateful workloads needing large EBS volumes
- PREFER Managed Node Groups + Karpenter over Fargate for cost-sensitive production workloads — Karpenter Spot often beats Fargate pricing by 50%
- USE Fargate profiles for dev/test workloads to eliminate node group management overhead in non-production environments

Trade-offs:
- Managed Node Groups: full control, supports all Kubernetes features, lower cost with Spot vs. you manage node OS updates (AWS handles via managed update, but you schedule it)
- Fargate: zero node management, per-pod billing, perfect isolation vs. 30-50% higher cost vs Spot, no DaemonSets, slower startup, 20GB ephemeral storage max
- Bottlerocket (OS for Managed Nodes): minimal attack surface, fast boot, CIS-hardened vs. limits in-node debugging tools (no package manager)
- AL2023 (Amazon Linux 2023): full ecosystem, familiar tooling vs. larger OS footprint vs. Bottlerocket

Anti-patterns:
- Running all workloads on EKS Fargate to avoid node management — Fargate pricing and constraints make it unsuitable as the primary compute plane for complex clusters
- Using self-managed node groups (manually managed EC2 Auto Scaling Groups) instead of Managed Node Groups — you lose AWS-managed node updates, health remediation, and EKS version alignment
- Not enabling Managed Node Group update config for maximum unavailability — default is 1, which slows cluster upgrades significantly for large node groups
- Running EKS control plane without any node compute strategy — control plane costs $72/month; if no nodes, workloads cannot schedule

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- EKS Best Practices: Managed Node Groups are the recommended compute plane — AWS manages node lifecycle, version updates, and health replacement
- Security Pillar: Bottlerocket OS for node groups provides CIS-hardened, minimal attack surface vs. general-purpose Amazon Linux
- Cost Optimization: Managed Node Groups + Karpenter Spot typically achieves 40-60% cost reduction vs. EKS Fargate for sustained workloads

Resource Requests and Limits — QoS Classes and Scheduling Accuracy

Resource requests tell the Kubernetes scheduler how much CPU/memory to reserve on a node. Resource limits cap the maximum a container can consume. Together, they determine the pod's Quality of Service (QoS) class: Guaranteed (requests = limits), Burstable (requests < limits), or BestEffort (no requests/limits). QoS class determines eviction priority under node memory pressure — BestEffort pods are evicted first. Correct resource configuration is the foundation of cluster stability. On EKS with Karpenter, accurate requests also determine correct node instance type selection — if requests are too low, Karpenter provisions nodes that are too small and workloads OOM-kill.

Decision rules:
- ALWAYS set both CPU and memory requests for every container — pods without requests are BestEffort and are the first to be evicted under memory pressure
- SET resource requests based on observed p75 usage from production metrics — not p95 or max (too wasteful) and not guesses
- SET memory limits = memory requests for critical pods (Guaranteed QoS) — prevents OOM kill surprises, ensures scheduler reservation matches actual usage
- SET CPU limits only for batch workloads that must not burst — for API pods, consider omitting CPU limits to allow CPU bursting on underutilized nodes (EKS Best Practices recommends this)
- USE LimitRange admission controller to set namespace-level default requests/limits — prevents new deployments from running without resource configuration
- USE Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) in recommendation mode to continuously suggest right-sized requests based on actual usage

Trade-offs:
- Guaranteed QoS (requests = limits): predictable performance, no eviction vs. wastes resources if actual usage is consistently below limits
- Burstable QoS (requests < limits): efficient resource utilization, allows CPU bursting vs. pod can be evicted under pressure, CPU throttling risk
- Omitting CPU limits: allows CPU bursting on idle nodes vs. a runaway process can consume all node CPU, causing noisy-neighbor impact
- VPA in auto mode: automatic right-sizing vs. VPA requires pod restarts to apply new requests — disruptive for stateless APIs

Anti-patterns:
- Setting requests very low and limits very high (e.g., request 10m CPU, limit 4 CPU) — Karpenter provisions a small node, pod OOM-kills on first traffic spike
- Setting memory limits lower than memory requests — Kubernetes immediately kills the pod (invalid configuration)
- Not using LimitRange in production namespaces — one developer deploys a pod without requests, creating a BestEffort pod that OOM-kills during a traffic spike
- Using identical resource profiles for all services — an ML inference container and a lightweight API proxy have wildly different resource needs

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Performance Efficiency: accurate resource requests enable correct Karpenter node sizing — prevents over-provisioning and under-provisioning
- Reliability Pillar: Guaranteed QoS prevents critical workloads from being evicted under node memory pressure
- EKS Best Practices: explicitly recommends omitting CPU limits for latency-sensitive workloads to allow CPU bursting on spare node capacity

Health Checks — Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes

Kubernetes uses three probe types to determine pod health. Liveness probe: if it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container — use for detecting deadlocks or hung processes. Readiness probe: if it fails, the pod is removed from Service endpoints and receives no traffic — use for detecting when the app is not ready to serve (dependent service unavailable, cache warming). Startup probe: allows slow-starting containers extra time before liveness kicks in — use for JVM applications, ML model loading, or any app with > 30 second startup time. Incorrectly configured probes cause either infinite pod restarts (liveness too aggressive) or traffic routed to unhealthy pods (readiness too lenient).

Decision rules:
- ALWAYS configure a readiness probe for every HTTP service — this is what prevents traffic from reaching pods during startup and graceful shutdown
- CONFIGURE a liveness probe for long-running services — detects deadlocks; set initialDelaySeconds generously (30-60s) to avoid restart loops during normal startup
- USE a startup probe for applications with > 30 second startup time — prevents liveness probe from killing the container while it is still starting
- USE HTTP GET probe for HTTP services, TCP socket probe for TCP services, exec probe (command) only as a last resort — exec probes create subprocesses and add overhead
- SET probe timeoutSeconds based on 99th percentile response time of the health endpoint — not the p50 — avoid false failures under load
- IMPLEMENT separate /health (liveness), /ready (readiness), and /startup endpoints in the application — each should check different conditions

Trade-offs:
- Aggressive liveness probe (short period, low failureThreshold): rapid recovery from deadlock vs. risk of restart loop on momentary slow responses under traffic spike
- Lenient readiness probe: fewer false positives vs. pods serve traffic before truly ready, causing errors for first N requests
- Startup probe: allows JVM warmup vs. longer time to detect a pod that is stuck and will never start
- Exec probe: can check app-specific conditions vs. creates OS subprocess per check interval, adds overhead on high-pod-count clusters

Anti-patterns:
- Using the same endpoint for both liveness and readiness — if the app is under load and readiness fails (correct behavior), liveness also triggers a restart (incorrect)
- Setting initialDelaySeconds too low for liveness — Kubernetes kills the pod before it finishes starting, triggering a restart loop that looks like an application crash
- No readiness probe on an API Deployment — during rolling update, pods receive traffic immediately on container start before the app has initialized its connection pool
- Liveness probe calling an external dependency (database, third-party API) — if the dependency is down, every pod in the cluster restarts simultaneously

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: readiness probes are the mechanism that makes ALB target group health checks meaningful — ALB routes only to ready pods
- EKS Best Practices: configure readiness probe before liveness; prefer HTTP probes; set appropriate thresholds based on p99 response time
- Operational Excellence: startup probe eliminates false-positive restarts during deployments — reduces MTTR noise

Observability — Metrics, Logs, and Traces on EKS

Production EKS observability requires three pillars: metrics (Prometheus + Grafana or CloudWatch Container Insights), logs (FluentBit to CloudWatch Logs or OpenSearch), and traces (AWS X-Ray or OpenTelemetry). Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus (AMP) and Amazon Managed Grafana (AMG) are the AWS-native managed replacements for self-hosted Prometheus/Grafana. The EKS Add-on for CloudWatch Observability deploys the CloudWatch agent and FluentBit as a DaemonSet, collecting node-level metrics and container logs automatically. The AI agent must select the observability stack based on team expertise, budget, and existing AWS service usage.

Decision rules:
- USE Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus (AMP) + Amazon Managed Grafana for new EKS clusters — eliminates Prometheus/Grafana operational overhead
- USE CloudWatch Container Insights for teams already invested in the CloudWatch ecosystem — provides node, pod, and container metrics with minimal setup
- DEPLOY FluentBit as a DaemonSet for log shipping — it is resource-efficient, supports multiple log outputs, and is the AWS-recommended log collector for EKS
- ENABLE AWS X-Ray for distributed tracing — instrument SDKs in application code, use X-Ray daemon sidecar or OpenTelemetry Collector as a DaemonSet
- SET Prometheus scrape intervals to 30s for production — 15s is only needed for high-cardinality troubleshooting and doubles storage cost
- DEFINE SLOs (Service Level Objectives) for each service: target error rate < 0.1%, p99 latency < 200ms — alert on SLO burn rate, not individual metric thresholds

Trade-offs:
- AMP + AMG: fully managed, scales automatically vs. higher cost than self-hosted Prometheus, AWS-locked observability stack
- Self-hosted Prometheus: full control, open-source, no vendor lock vs. requires storage management, HA setup, retention policies — significant operational overhead
- CloudWatch Container Insights: zero setup for basic metrics, native AWS integration vs. limited query language (CW Logs Insights is not PromQL), higher cost at scale
- OpenTelemetry Collector: vendor-neutral, future-proof instrumentation vs. more complex setup than AWS-specific X-Ray SDK

Anti-patterns:
- Not collecting container-level metrics (only node metrics) — node metrics hide pod-level resource exhaustion and application-level errors
- Using kubectl logs for production debugging — no persistence, no search, no aggregation; use CloudWatch Logs or OpenSearch
- Setting Prometheus retention to 30 days on EKS cluster storage — Prometheus TSDB is not designed for long-term storage; use Thanos, Cortex, or AMP remote write
- Alerting on every individual metric threshold — creates alert fatigue; alert on SLO burn rate (error budget consumption) instead

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Operational Excellence: CloudWatch Container Insights + FluentBit is the AWS-native, minimal-setup observability stack for EKS
- EKS Best Practices: use Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and Amazon Managed Grafana for production-grade metrics at scale
- Reliability Pillar: SLO-based alerting on error budget burn rate is the Well-Architected approach to reducing alert noise

RBAC — Role-Based Access Control for EKS

Kubernetes RBAC controls what API actions subjects (users, groups, service accounts) can perform on which resources. On EKS, RBAC integrates with IAM via the aws-auth ConfigMap (legacy) or EKS Access Entries (new, recommended). IAM entities (users, roles) are mapped to Kubernetes RBAC groups or cluster-level permissions. The EKS Best Practices Guide emphasizes: one IAM role per purpose, separate cluster admin from developer access, use namespaced Roles (not ClusterRoles) for application teams, and audit all RBAC bindings regularly. Kubernetes service accounts used by pods should have minimal RBAC — ideally no Kubernetes RBAC permissions at all, just IRSA for AWS API access.

Decision rules:
- USE EKS Access Entries (not aws-auth ConfigMap) for new clusters — Access Entries are API-driven, auditable, and managed via IaC without manual ConfigMap editing
- MAP IAM roles to Kubernetes RBAC groups — never map individual IAM users; roles are manageable and auditable
- GRANT application teams namespace-scoped Roles (not ClusterRoles) — developers should deploy to their namespace, not see other namespaces
- RESERVE system:masters group (cluster admin equivalent) for the platform team IAM role only — no CI/CD pipelines should have cluster admin
- GRANT CI/CD pipeline IAM roles only the RBAC permissions needed: create/update/delete Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps in specific namespaces — not get nodes, list secrets cluster-wide
- USE kubectl auth can-i --as system:serviceaccount:namespace:sa-name to audit what permissions a service account has before deploying

Trade-offs:
- EKS Access Entries: API-driven, Terraform-manageable vs. new feature, some organizations' legacy tooling may not support it yet
- aws-auth ConfigMap (legacy): widely documented, battle-tested vs. manual editing can corrupt the ConfigMap and lock out all cluster access
- Broad ClusterRole: simple initial setup vs. violates least-privilege, one misconfigured service account can read cluster secrets
- Namespace-scoped Roles: strict isolation vs. more Terraform/YAML to manage per team/namespace

Anti-patterns:
- Editing aws-auth ConfigMap manually in production — a YAML indentation error can lock all IAM users out of the cluster, requiring EC2 console rescue
- Granting developers cluster-admin — they can read secrets in all namespaces, delete cluster-critical resources, and elevate privileges
- Using the default service account with no explicit permissions and no automountServiceAccountToken: false — the default SA has no permissions but its token is auto-mounted and can be used to query the Kubernetes API
- Not auditing RBAC regularly — unused bindings accumulate over time, increasing the blast radius of a compromised service account

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: EKS Access Entries + IAM role mapping implements the AWS principle of using IAM for identity and Kubernetes RBAC for authorization
- EKS Best Practices: EKS Access Entries replace aws-auth ConfigMap — AWS-managed, auditable, safe from manual editing errors
- Operational Excellence: Terraform-managed Access Entries create an auditable, version-controlled RBAC configuration

Network Policies — Pod-to-Pod Traffic Isolation

By default, all pods in a Kubernetes cluster can communicate with all other pods — no isolation. Network Policies are Kubernetes resources that define which pods can communicate with which other pods and external endpoints. They are enforced by the CNI plugin. On EKS, two options exist: the VPC CNI plugin with Kubernetes Network Policy enforcement (added in EKS 1.25+) and the Calico network policy engine. Network Policies are the primary mechanism for micro-segmentation in EKS — ensuring that a compromised frontend pod cannot directly reach the database pod.

Decision rules:
- IMPLEMENT Network Policies for any cluster running multi-tenant workloads or sensitive data — the default allow-all is not acceptable for production security
- START with a default-deny-all ingress policy in each namespace, then add explicit allow rules — allowlist model is safer than denylist
- USE Network Policies to enforce service-to-service communication contracts: frontend → API allowed, frontend → database denied
- ENABLE EKS native Network Policy enforcement (VPC CNI) for new clusters — it uses eBPF in the kernel, no additional CNI installation required
- USE Calico Network Policy for: existing clusters where VPC CNI enforcement is not available, or when egress Network Policies must restrict DNS/external access by pod
- TEST Network Policies in a staging environment — a misconfigured policy that blocks service-to-service traffic causes silent failures, not errors

Trade-offs:
- VPC CNI native enforcement: no extra CNI to manage, eBPF-based performance vs. newer feature, limited to EKS clusters with VPC CNI ≥ 1.14
- Calico: mature, rich policy language, works across distributions vs. additional DaemonSet to manage, Calico-specific CRDs
- Default-deny: strong security baseline vs. can block legitimate traffic if allowlist is incomplete — requires thorough service dependency mapping
- No Network Policies: simple, zero overhead vs. complete east-west traffic freedom, compromised pod can reach all services

Anti-patterns:
- Relying solely on security groups for pod isolation — security groups operate at the ENI level (per-node or per-pod with VPC CNI), not per-Kubernetes-label; network policies provide finer control
- Writing Network Policies only for ingress and ignoring egress — a compromised pod with no egress policy can exfiltrate data to any external endpoint
- Not labeling pods consistently — Network Policies select pods by labels; inconsistent labeling creates unintended policy gaps
- Applying the same Network Policy to all namespaces — different environments (dev, staging, prod) have different trust boundaries

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: Network Policies implement micro-segmentation — the AWS Well-Architected 'defense in depth' pattern at the pod level
- EKS Best Practices: enable Network Policies to complement VPC security groups — Network Policies provide Kubernetes-aware isolation that SGs cannot
- EKS Blueprints: Network Policy enforcement is listed as a required security add-on in EKS production cluster blueprints

EKS Security Hardening — Pod Security, CIS Benchmark, and Supply Chain

Comprehensive EKS security hardening operates at four layers: cluster configuration (control plane logging, private API endpoint, envelope encryption), node security (Bottlerocket OS, IMDSv2 enforcement, no SSH), pod security (Kubernetes Pod Security Standards — Restricted profile, no privileged containers), and supply chain security (ECR image scanning, admission control via OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno). The EKS Best Practices Security Guide maps each control to the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark v1.8. The AI agent must ensure that security is not an afterthought — it is embedded in the cluster provisioning Terraform and enforced at admission time.

Decision rules:
- ENABLE EKS control plane logging for all log types (api, audit, authenticator, controllerManager, scheduler) — sent to CloudWatch Logs for forensic analysis
- USE private API endpoint for production EKS clusters — the Kubernetes API should not be accessible from the internet; use VPN or bastion for admin access
- ENFORCE IMDSv2 (hop limit 1) on EKS node launch templates — prevents containers from using IMDS to steal node EC2 credentials
- APPLY Pod Security Standards at namespace level: Baseline for most workloads, Restricted for sensitive workloads — enforced via Pod Security Admission (built into Kubernetes 1.25+)
- DEPLOY OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno for custom admission policies: require image tags (no :latest), require resource limits, require non-root user
- ENABLE ECR image scanning (Enhanced Scanning with Amazon Inspector) for all repositories — block deployments of images with CRITICAL CVEs via OPA/Kyverno admission policy
- ROTATE the EKS cluster certificate annually and when team member leaves — use EKS rotate-certificate API

Trade-offs:
- Private API endpoint: strong security posture vs. requires VPN or bastion for kubectl access — operational complexity for development teams
- Pod Security Standards (Restricted): blocks privileged containers, rootless requirement vs. some third-party add-ons require privileged pods (may need exception namespaces)
- OPA Gatekeeper: powerful policy language (Rego), audit mode vs. Rego has a steep learning curve; Kyverno uses Kubernetes-native YAML and is easier to adopt
- ECR Enhanced Scanning: continuous CVE monitoring vs. Scanner may block deployments on library vulnerabilities that are not exploitable in your context

Anti-patterns:
- Public EKS API endpoint without IP allowlisting — the Kubernetes API is exposed to the internet, any stolen kubeconfig gives full cluster access
- Running containers as root (UID 0) — if a container breakout occurs, the attacker has root on the node
- Allowing :latest image tags in production — non-deterministic, cannot roll back, no image digest pinning
- No admission control — developers can deploy containers with privileged: true, hostNetwork: true, and no resource limits
- Not patching EKS cluster version regularly — EKS versions reach end-of-support; unpatched clusters accumulate CVEs in Kubernetes API server and etcd

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: private API endpoint + control plane logging + IMDSv2 + KMS envelope encryption addresses all four EKS security baselines in the Well-Architected Framework
- EKS Best Practices Security Guide: maps directly to CIS Kubernetes Benchmark v1.8 controls — use this guide as the authoritative security checklist
- EKS Blueprints: Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper, ECR scanning, and private endpoint are all standard components of the EKS Blueprint reference architecture

Terraform Resources

Resources are the fundamental building blocks of Terraform infrastructure. Each resource block maps to one real-world infrastructure object. Resource lifecycle, dependencies, and ordering are managed by Terraform's dependency graph. Understanding implicit vs. explicit dependencies and lifecycle hooks (create_before_destroy, prevent_destroy, ignore_changes) is critical for production-grade infrastructure.

Decision rules:
- USE implicit dependencies (reference expressions) over explicit depends_on — Terraform resolves them more efficiently
- USE depends_on ONLY when a dependency exists that Terraform cannot detect through references (e.g., IAM policy propagation timing)
- APPLY create_before_destroy lifecycle rule for resources that cannot have downtime during replacement (e.g., Auto Scaling Launch Templates, TLS certificates)
- APPLY prevent_destroy to stateful resources: RDS instances, S3 buckets with data, EFS volumes
- USE ignore_changes for attributes managed outside Terraform (e.g., AMI IDs managed by autoscaling, tags set by AWS Config)

Trade-offs:
- Granular resources: full control and visibility vs. more code and higher state complexity
- Using AWS modules vs. raw resources: faster development vs. less control over individual settings
- Lifecycle rules: prevents accidental deletion vs. may require manual intervention for replacements

Anti-patterns:
- Creating resources without tagging — violates cost attribution and compliance requirements
- Hardcoding resource names with no randomness suffix when a resource must be unique — causes naming conflicts on recreation
- Not using count or for_each for repeated patterns — leads to copy-paste IaC with drift risk
- Importing existing resources without a plan to bring them fully under Terraform management

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Operational Excellence: lifecycle rules prevent unintended downtime
- Reliability: prevent_destroy on stateful resources reduces blast radius of accidents
- Cost Optimization: tagging strategy enables cost allocation per team/environment

Terraform Modules

Modules are reusable, composable units of Terraform configuration. They encapsulate related resources with a defined interface (input variables and outputs). Modules enforce consistency across environments and teams. There are two categories: root modules (what you execute) and child modules (what you call). The terraform-aws-modules GitHub organization provides battle-tested, AWS-specific modules like terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws that embed production defaults.

Decision rules:
- CREATE a module when the same infrastructure pattern repeats across 2+ environments or teams
- USE public registry modules (terraform-aws-modules) for foundational patterns: VPC, EKS, RDS — they embed AWS best practices
- BUILD internal modules for business-specific patterns: application stacks, compliance baselines
- COMPOSE modules from smaller modules rather than monolithic super-modules — easier to test and maintain
- VERSION pin all module sources — both registry modules (~> 20.0) and Git sources (?ref=v2.1.0)
- EXPOSE only the variables that callers need to change — default all production-safe values inside the module

Trade-offs:
- Module abstraction: reduced duplication vs. abstraction cost — debugging requires understanding multiple layers
- Public registry modules: fast adoption of best practices vs. opinionated defaults may not fit all use cases
- Deep module nesting: clean separation vs. difficult to trace resource origins in plans
- Module versioning: stability guarantee vs. delayed adoption of upstream security fixes

Anti-patterns:
- Creating a single God-module that contains all infrastructure — untestable, unmaintainable, prevents independent deployments
- Calling modules without pinned versions — upstream changes break your infrastructure on next init
- Exposing every resource attribute as a module variable — creates a passthrough module with no value
- Mixing module outputs with direct resource references in the same root module — creates unclear ownership
- Duplicating AWS modules from public registry internally without adding value — maintenance burden with no benefit

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Operational Excellence: modules enforce standards across teams, reduce human error
- Security Pillar: security baselines encoded in modules cannot be bypassed per-deployment
- Cost Optimization: standardized modules prevent over-provisioned outliers

Remote State Management — S3 + DynamoDB

Terraform state is the source of truth for managed infrastructure. In production, state must be stored remotely (S3) with encryption, versioning, and distributed locking (DynamoDB). State isolation between environments prevents a failed prod deployment from corrupting staging state. State should be organized by the blast radius of change — network state separate from application state.

Decision rules:
- ALWAYS use remote S3 backend in production — local state is a single point of failure and a security risk
- ENABLE S3 versioning on the state bucket — enables rollback to previous known-good state
- ENABLE S3 server-side encryption (AES-256 or KMS) for state at rest — state contains sensitive values
- CREATE a DynamoDB table for state locking — prevents concurrent applies from corrupting state
- SEPARATE state files by: environment (dev/staging/prod) AND layer (network, compute, data) — limits blast radius
- USE terraform_remote_state data source to share outputs across state files rather than duplicating resources
- RESTRICT S3 state bucket access via IAM — only CI/CD roles and authorized engineers should read/write

Trade-offs:
- State isolation by layer: small blast radius vs. more state files to manage and coordinate
- Single monolithic state: simple coordination vs. any failure/lock blocks all deployments
- KMS encryption: strong security vs. additional cost and KMS API dependency
- State locking: prevents corruption vs. a crashed apply holds the lock until DynamoDB TTL expires

Anti-patterns:
- Committing state files to Git — exposes secrets and resource IDs, creates merge conflicts
- Using a single state file for all environments — a plan mistake in prod destroys the ability to manage dev
- Not enabling state versioning — no recovery path after accidental terraform destroy
- Sharing state files across teams with different deployment cadences — constant lock contention
- Storing the state bucket and lock table in the same account as the managed infrastructure without separate access control

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: encrypted state, least-privilege access to state bucket
- Reliability Pillar: state versioning enables recovery from accidental destruction
- Operational Excellence: state isolation by layer enables independent team deployments

Variables and Outputs

Variables define the interface of a Terraform configuration, allowing reuse across environments. Outputs expose resource attributes for consumption by other modules or root configurations. A disciplined variable strategy separates environment-specific values (tfvars files) from module defaults, and sensitive values from non-sensitive ones. Outputs should expose exactly what downstream consumers need — not raw resource objects.

Decision rules:
- DECLARE variable types explicitly — prevents runtime errors from type mismatches
- MARK variables as sensitive = true for passwords, tokens, and private keys — prevents Terraform from printing them in logs
- USE .tfvars files per environment (dev.tfvars, prod.tfvars) — never commit prod values to Git
- SET safe default values for optional variables, requiring only what must differ per environment
- OUTPUT the minimum surface area: IDs, ARNs, DNS names — not full resource objects
- USE output descriptions — downstream teams and modules need to know what an output represents
- VALIDATE variables with custom validation blocks when the range of valid values is constrained

Trade-offs:
- Strict typing: catches errors early vs. requires more upfront definition work
- Sensitive marking: protects secrets in logs vs. makes debugging harder when values are hidden
- Many fine-grained variables: highly flexible module interface vs. complex caller experience
- Defaulting everything: fast to call vs. hides important configuration that should be intentional

Anti-patterns:
- Passing secrets as plain-text variables in tfvars committed to version control
- Using string type for all variables — loses validation and readability benefits
- Outputting entire resource objects — exposes unintended attributes and creates tight coupling
- Not validating list or map variable lengths when the module expects specific counts
- Using variable names that shadow Terraform built-in functions or keywords

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: sensitive variables prevent credential leakage in CI/CD logs
- Operational Excellence: typed and validated variables reduce deployment errors

Environment Separation Strategy — dev / staging / prod

Environment separation is the practice of maintaining fully isolated infrastructure stacks per environment, preventing changes in one environment from affecting another. The gold standard uses separate AWS accounts per environment (AWS Organizations) to provide hard blast radius boundaries. At minimum, separate Terraform state, VPCs, and IAM roles must exist per environment. A staging environment must be production-equivalent to be useful for validation.

Decision rules:
- USE separate AWS accounts for prod vs. non-prod environments when budget allows — account-level isolation is the strongest boundary
- USE separate Terraform state files per environment — never share state between dev and prod
- MAKE staging infrastructure topology identical to prod — same instance types, same AZ count, same security group rules
- ALLOW instance sizing differences between environments but never topology differences — staging in 2 AZs while prod is 3 is acceptable
- RESTRICT prod account access to break-glass scenarios only — all prod changes must go through CI/CD pipeline, not console
- DEPLOY infrastructure changes through environments in sequence: dev → staging → prod with automated gates
- USE separate Terraform workspaces ONLY for ephemeral environments — not for persistent environment separation

Trade-offs:
- Separate accounts: strongest isolation vs. higher AWS Organizations overhead, cross-account networking complexity
- Identical staging topology: accurate pre-prod testing vs. 2x infrastructure cost for staging
- Strict pipeline gates: prevents bad deployments reaching prod vs. slower deployment cycle
- Shared account multi-VPC: simpler IAM vs. blast radius extends across environments on IAM misconfiguration

Anti-patterns:
- Sharing a VPC between dev and prod — a misconfigured route or security group can expose prod data to dev
- Making staging infrastructure materially different from prod — bugs that only reproduce in prod become hard to diagnose
- Allowing direct console access to production for routine changes — changes bypass IaC, create drift, cannot be rolled back
- Using Terraform workspaces for dev/prod separation — see workspace anti-pattern entry
- Deploying to prod without a successful staging run — eliminates pre-prod validation value

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: account-level isolation prevents cross-environment credential and data exposure
- Operational Excellence: pipeline-driven deployments with staged rollouts reduce change failure rate
- Reliability: staging validates changes before they reach production workloads

Terraform Module Structuring — Layered Architecture

A well-structured Terraform repository separates infrastructure into layers with clearly defined ownership and change cadence. Network infrastructure changes rarely; compute changes frequently; application configuration changes continuously. Separating these layers allows fast application deployments without re-planning slow-changing network infrastructure. The standard layering is: core/network layer → platform layer (EKS/ECS/RDS) → application layer.

Decision rules:
- LAYER infrastructure into: 00-network (VPC, subnets, TGW), 10-platform (EKS/ECS, RDS, ElastiCache), 20-application (services, ALBs, DNS records)
- DEPLOY lower layers less frequently — network changes are rare; application changes are daily
- CONSUME lower-layer outputs via terraform_remote_state or SSM Parameter Store — never duplicate resources across layers
- STRUCTURE module directory as: modules/<name>/{main.tf, variables.tf, outputs.tf, versions.tf} — consistent interface
- KEEP root modules thin — root modules orchestrate calls to reusable child modules, not implement resources directly
- CREATE a separate live/ directory for root modules and a modules/ directory for reusable modules — Terragrunt pattern

Trade-offs:
- Fine-grained layers: fast targeted applies vs. more state files and more coordination
- Monorepo vs. multi-repo for modules: easy cross-module changes vs. clearer ownership boundaries
- Deep module nesting: clean abstraction vs. difficult to trace resource lineage in plans
- Terragrunt for DRY configs: eliminates root module duplication vs. additional tooling dependency

Anti-patterns:
- Single root module for all infrastructure — slow plans (1000+ resources), high blast radius, team conflicts
- Root modules with direct resource definitions instead of module calls — kills reusability
- Network resources and application resources in the same state file — network failure blocks application deployments
- Circular module dependencies — module A calls module B which calls module A
- Not documenting module interfaces (variables.tf descriptions) — forces code reading to understand inputs

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Operational Excellence: layered deployment reduces deployment risk and change failure rate
- Reliability: infrastructure layers can be independently recovered when a layer fails

Secrets Management — SSM Parameter Store vs. AWS Secrets Manager

Secrets management is the practice of storing and distributing sensitive configuration (passwords, API keys, certificates) without exposing them in code, environment variables, or Terraform state. AWS provides two services: SSM Parameter Store (free for standard parameters, KMS-encrypted SecureString) and Secrets Manager (paid, rotation support, cross-account access, fine-grained IAM). The choice depends on rotation requirements and secret value.

Decision rules:
- USE Secrets Manager WHEN: automatic rotation is required (RDS passwords, API keys), cross-account secret sharing needed, or secret value justifies the cost (~$0.40/secret/month)
- USE SSM Parameter Store SecureString WHEN: configuration values, feature flags, simple API keys without rotation, cost-sensitive environments
- NEVER store secrets in Terraform state — use SSM/Secrets Manager data sources to inject at runtime, not plan time
- NEVER store secrets in environment variables in ECS task definitions or Lambda configuration in plaintext — reference Secrets Manager ARN instead
- ENABLE automatic rotation for all database passwords via Secrets Manager rotation Lambda
- USE separate secrets per environment — dev and prod must never share a secret ARN
- AUDIT secret access with CloudTrail — every GetSecretValue call should be logged

Trade-offs:
- Secrets Manager: automatic rotation, rich IAM vs. $0.40/secret/month — significant cost at scale
- SSM SecureString: free (standard), KMS encryption vs. no native rotation, less fine-grained access control
- Runtime injection: secrets never in state vs. application startup dependency on secrets service availability
- Secrets in env vars: simple to implement vs. visible in process list, container inspect output, and logs

Anti-patterns:
- Hardcoding secrets in Terraform tfvars files committed to Git — permanent credential exposure in git history
- Storing plaintext secrets in SSM Standard Parameter (not SecureString) — unencrypted at rest
- Sharing a single database password across all environments — breach in dev exposes prod credential
- Not rotating secrets after a potential exposure event — treating rotation as optional
- Using Terraform to write secrets into the state file via aws_ssm_parameter resource with sensitive=false

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: secrets management is explicitly required by the AWS Security pillar for credential protection
- Operational Excellence: automatic rotation reduces manual credential management toil

AWS Resource Tagging Strategy

Tags are key-value metadata on AWS resources. A consistent tagging strategy enables cost allocation by team/project, security policy enforcement via IAM conditions, automated compliance checks, and operational runbooks (e.g., auto-start/stop dev resources). Without tags, AWS cost reports are unreadable and security audits cannot identify resource ownership. Tags must be enforced at provisioning time, not added retroactively.

Decision rules:
- ENFORCE minimum required tags on all resources: Environment, Project, Team, ManagedBy, CostCenter
- USE Environment tag values consistently: dev, staging, prod — not Dev, Development, PROD
- SET ManagedBy = terraform for all Terraform-managed resources — enables drift detection
- ADD Name tag to all resources — human-readable identifier in the console
- USE AWS Organizations Tag Policy to enforce tag keys and valid values across all accounts
- PROPAGATE tags from Auto Scaling Groups to launched EC2 instances using propagate_at_launch = true
- USE provider default_tags block in Terraform to apply common tags to all resources without repetition

Trade-offs:
- Many tags: rich metadata vs. tag limit of 50 per resource, management overhead
- Enforced tag policy: compliance vs. blocks resource creation if tags are missing — requires team training
- provider default_tags: DRY tagging vs. individual resources cannot override inherited tags easily

Anti-patterns:
- Inconsistent tag values across teams — 'production', 'prod', 'PROD' make cost reports require manual normalization
- Only tagging some resource types — cost allocation gaps for untagged resources are untraceable
- Not tagging at resource creation — retroactive tagging is operationally expensive and error-prone
- Using tags for access control without enforcement — tags can be modified by anyone with resource update permission

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Cost Optimization: cost allocation tags enable showback and chargeback per team/project
- Operational Excellence: ownership tags accelerate incident response by identifying responsible team
- Security Pillar: tag-based IAM conditions can restrict operations to environment-appropriate resources

Cost Optimization Patterns — Reserved Capacity and Right-Sizing

AWS cost optimization is a continuous process, not a one-time activity. The biggest levers are: Reserved Instance / Savings Plans for predictable workloads, Spot instances for fault-tolerant workloads, right-sizing to eliminate over-provisioned resources, and lifecycle policies to delete unused resources. The AWS Well-Architected Cost Optimization pillar emphasizes that cost should be a first-class metric, visible to engineering teams.

Decision rules:
- PURCHASE 1-year Savings Plans for stable workloads (>70% utilization baseline) — delivers 30-40% savings over On-Demand
- PURCHASE 3-year Reserved Instances for database instances (RDS) with known longevity — up to 60% savings
- USE Spot instances for: batch jobs, EKS non-critical node groups, dev/staging environments — 60-90% savings
- RIGHT-SIZE instances after 2 weeks of CloudWatch metrics — use AWS Compute Optimizer recommendations
- ENABLE S3 Intelligent-Tiering for buckets with unknown access patterns — auto-moves objects to cheaper tiers
- SET S3 lifecycle policies to transition logs/backups to S3 Glacier after 30 days, expire after 365 days
- DELETE unattached EBS volumes, unused Elastic IPs, and idle load balancers — these generate cost with zero value
- USE CloudWatch Cost Anomaly Detection to alert on unexpected spend increases

Trade-offs:
- Reserved Instances: guaranteed savings vs. upfront commitment — inflexible if workload changes
- Savings Plans: more flexible than RIs (Compute Savings Plans apply across EC2 family/region) vs. slightly lower max discount
- Spot instances: maximum savings vs. requires application fault tolerance design upfront
- Over-provisioning for headroom: operational safety vs. wasted spend — use auto-scaling instead

Anti-patterns:
- Paying On-Demand for workloads that have been running >3 months — most expensive option for predictable workloads
- Not setting S3 lifecycle policies on log buckets — logs grow indefinitely at S3 Standard pricing
- Leaving development environments running 24/7 — dev environments should stop at end of business hours
- Using large RDS instances 'just in case' without Performance Insights to validate the need
- Purchasing Reserved Instances without first right-sizing — locking into wrong instance type

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Cost Optimization Pillar: this entry directly implements the Cost Optimization pillar's practice areas
- Operational Excellence: cost visibility enables teams to make informed architecture decisions

Observability Architecture — Metrics, Logs, Traces

Production observability requires three pillars: metrics (CloudWatch, dashboards), logs (CloudWatch Logs, structured logging), and distributed traces (AWS X-Ray or OpenTelemetry). Without observability, incident MTTR increases dramatically because engineers cannot distinguish between application bugs, infrastructure failures, and dependency issues. Observability must be designed into the infrastructure, not added after incidents.

Decision rules:
- ENABLE CloudWatch Container Insights for ECS and EKS — provides CPU, memory, network, and disk metrics per pod
- CONFIGURE structured JSON logging for all applications — enables CloudWatch Logs Insights queries
- SET CloudWatch alarms for: high CPU (>80%), memory pressure, error rate (5xx > threshold), DB connection count
- ENABLE X-Ray tracing on ALB, Lambda, ECS tasks, and API Gateway — provides end-to-end request tracing
- USE CloudWatch Log Groups with retention policies — default is infinite retention (expensive and unnecessary)
- CREATE CloudWatch dashboards per service — single-pane visibility reduces investigation time
- SET log retention to: 7 days for debug logs, 30 days for application logs, 90 days for audit/security logs, 1 year for compliance logs

Trade-offs:
- Full observability: fast incident response vs. CloudWatch Logs costs can be significant at high log volume
- Structured logging: queryable, parseable vs. requires application code changes and discipline
- X-Ray tracing: performance bottleneck identification vs. sampling rate tuning required to control cost
- Long log retention: compliance support vs. CloudWatch Logs storage cost

Anti-patterns:
- No CloudWatch alarms — incidents are discovered by customers before engineering teams
- Logging without retention policies — log storage becomes a significant monthly cost silently
- Not correlating metrics, logs, and traces — forces manual investigation across multiple tools
- Using print/console.log for structured data — unqueryable in CloudWatch Logs Insights

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Operational Excellence Pillar: observability is the foundation of responding to events and improving processes
- Reliability Pillar: metric-based alarms trigger automated and manual recovery procedures

Disaster Recovery — RTO/RPO and Strategy Selection

Disaster Recovery (DR) defines how quickly a system can recover (RTO — Recovery Time Objective) and how much data loss is acceptable (RPO — Recovery Point Objective). AWS provides four DR patterns at increasing cost and complexity: backup-and-restore, pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active-active. The DR strategy must be chosen based on business requirements, not technical preferences.

Decision rules:
- DEFINE RTO and RPO with business stakeholders before designing DR — do not assume technical preferences
- USE Backup-and-Restore WHEN: RTO hours acceptable, RPO hours acceptable, cost sensitivity high — lowest DR cost
- USE Pilot Light WHEN: RTO 10-30 minutes acceptable, core data is replicated but compute is off — moderate cost
- USE Warm Standby WHEN: RTO minutes acceptable, RPO seconds, business-critical applications — significant cost
- USE Multi-Site Active-Active WHEN: RTO seconds/zero downtime, RPO near-zero, mission-critical revenue-generating systems — highest cost
- ENABLE RDS automated backups with point-in-time recovery — minimum DR for all database workloads
- TEST DR procedures quarterly — untested DR plans fail at the worst possible time
- USE AWS Backup service to centralize backup policies across RDS, EFS, EC2, and DynamoDB

Trade-offs:
- Active-Active: zero-downtime DR vs. 10-20x cost of backup-and-restore, complex data synchronization
- Warm Standby: minutes RTO vs. paying for duplicate running infrastructure at 50% capacity
- Pilot Light: cheap vs. 10-30 minute RTO includes provisioning time that may be unacceptable
- Cross-region vs. cross-AZ DR: protects against region failure vs. 10-100x higher data transfer costs

Anti-patterns:
- No DR plan for production databases — data loss is unacceptable in most business contexts
- DR plan that has never been tested — theoretical DR is not DR
- Assuming multi-AZ RDS is DR — Multi-AZ protects against AZ failure but not region failure or data corruption
- DR in the same region as primary — regional failure affects both primary and DR simultaneously

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Reliability Pillar: DR planning is a core reliability requirement
- Operational Excellence: regular DR testing is a required operational practice

CI/CD for Terraform — Pipeline Architecture

Terraform changes in production must go through an automated pipeline that enforces validation, planning, and approval gates. The pipeline prevents human error from direct apply operations, enforces policy checks (Checkov, tfsec, OPA), and creates an audit trail of all infrastructure changes. The Terraform plan output must be reviewed before apply, especially for destructive changes.

Decision rules:
- STRUCTURE pipeline as: lint/validate → plan (with saved planfile) → review gate → apply from planfile
- RUN terraform fmt check, terraform validate, and tflint in the lint stage — fast feedback before expensive plan
- RUN tfsec or Checkov on every plan — catches security misconfigurations before they reach AWS
- REQUIRE human approval for prod apply, especially when plan shows resource deletion or replacement
- SAVE terraform plan output as artifact — apply must use the exact same plan that was reviewed
- USE OIDC federation for CI/CD AWS authentication — eliminates long-lived IAM access keys in CI secrets
- BLOCK apply on main branch without passing tests — no exceptions for 'quick hotfixes'
- NOTIFY on all plan outputs that include resource destruction — proactive awareness before approval

Trade-offs:
- Approval gates: safety vs. deployment velocity — automate approval for dev, manual for prod
- Plan artifact: apply from reviewed plan vs. small plan/apply time gap allows AWS state to drift between them
- OIDC: no static credentials vs. more complex initial setup
- Full policy scanning: catches every misconfiguration vs. slower pipeline and false positives requiring tuning

Anti-patterns:
- Running terraform apply in CI without saving and reviewing the plan first — apply may do something different than expected
- Storing AWS credentials as CI/CD static secrets — rotate risk, blast radius on breach
- No policy scanning in pipeline — security misconfigurations reach production
- Allowing direct terraform apply from developer machines to production — no audit trail, no approval gate
- Not testing infrastructure modules — changes break downstream consumers silently

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Operational Excellence: automated pipelines with gates reduce change failure rate and improve audit capability
- Security Pillar: policy scanning in pipeline enforces security baseline consistently

Terraform Remote State Backend — S3 + DynamoDB Locking

Defines the production-standard Terraform remote state backend: an S3 bucket stores the terraform.tfstate file and a DynamoDB table provides state locking so two engineers or CI runs cannot apply simultaneously. The backend infrastructure is created once by a bootstrap configuration, after which state is migrated to the remote backend with `terraform init -migrate-state`. The S3 backend block (bucket, key, region, encrypt, dynamodb_table) is placed in backend.tf/versions.tf of every consuming module, not in main.tf.

When to use:
- Use for any Terraform managed by more than one engineer or by CI/CD — local state does not support locking or sharing
- Run the bootstrap configuration ONCE to create the bucket and lock table, then migrate state to the remote backend
- Use a per-workspace state key of the form `${var.environment}/${var.component}/terraform.tfstate` (e.g. prod/vpc/terraform.tfstate, staging/rds/terraform.tfstate) to isolate state per environment and component

Best practices:
- Enable S3 bucket versioning so any previous state file can be restored after a bad apply
- Set `prevent_destroy = true` on both the state bucket and the lock table so `terraform destroy` cannot delete them accidentally
- Use DynamoDB billing_mode PAY_PER_REQUEST with a single LockID (String) hash key — no capacity planning required for the lock table
- Keep the backend block in backend.tf or versions.tf (not main.tf) and pin the AWS provider (~> 5.0) and required_version (>= 1.5.0)

Security considerations:
- Enable server-side encryption on the state bucket (AES256, or a KMS key ARN for stricter control) — state files contain resource attributes and sometimes secrets
- Block ALL public access on the state bucket (block_public_acls, block_public_policy, ignore_public_acls, restrict_public_buckets) — state must never be public
- Grant the CI/CD role a least-privilege IAM policy scoped to exactly the state bucket (s3:GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject/ListBucket) and the lock table (dynamodb:GetItem/PutItem/DeleteItem/DescribeTable) — not account-wide S3 or DynamoDB access

Terraform resources: terraform { backend "s3" { bucket=..., key="${env}/${component}/terraform.tfstate", region=..., encrypt=true, dynamodb_table="terraform-state-locks" } } plus aws_s3_bucket (versioning + SSE + public_access_block + prevent_destroy) and aws_dynamodb_table (PAY_PER_REQUEST, LockID hash key, prevent_destroy).

Monolith Infrastructure Pattern

The monolith infrastructure pattern deploys a complete application stack (VPC, compute, database, load balancer) as a single Terraform root module or tightly coupled set of modules. It is appropriate for single-team, single-application contexts where deployment coordination is simple and the application itself is a monolith. It is the correct starting point for new projects but must be planned for extraction before team growth.

Decision rules:
- CHOOSE monolith infrastructure WHEN: single team, single application, early-stage project, team size < 5 engineers
- CHOOSE monolith infrastructure WHEN: application is a monolith and microservices decomposition is not planned
- STRUCTURE monolith infrastructure as: VPC module + compute module + data module in a single root module
- PLAN module boundaries even in a monolith — clean module interfaces allow future extraction to separate state files
- ACCEPT monolith infrastructure complexity until you feel the pain — do not pre-optimize for microservices
- MIGRATE away from monolith infrastructure WHEN: > 2 teams deploying independently, > 50 Terraform resources in one state file, plan time > 5 minutes

Trade-offs:
- Monolith infra: simple coordination, one deployment unit vs. any change requires full plan, high blast radius
- Monolith infra: fast initial development vs. becomes a bottleneck when teams deploy independently
- Early extraction: future-proof vs. YAGNI — premature decomposition creates coordination overhead without benefit

Anti-patterns:
- Keeping monolith infrastructure beyond team/application scale — plan times grow to 20+ minutes, deployment conflicts increase
- No module boundaries in monolith — resources directly in root module makes future extraction painful
- Multiple teams sharing a monolith state file — any team's merge blocks all other teams' deployments
- Monolith infrastructure for microservices applications — compute layer changes require network layer plan

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Operational Excellence: starting with monolith and extracting when pain is felt avoids premature complexity
- Cost Optimization: monolith infrastructure reduces overhead cost of managing many state files early in project lifecycle

Microservices Infrastructure Pattern

The microservices infrastructure pattern separates infrastructure by service ownership, change cadence, and blast radius. Each service team owns their Terraform modules for application-layer resources. Platform teams own shared infrastructure (VPC, EKS/ECS cluster, RDS). This mirrors the Conway's Law alignment where team structure should match system structure. Services consume shared platform outputs via terraform_remote_state or SSM.

Decision rules:
- CHOOSE microservices infrastructure WHEN: multiple independent teams, services deploy at different cadences, or application has >10 distinct services
- SEPARATE infrastructure into: platform layer (shared EKS/ECS, VPC, databases) and service layer (per-service ALB rules, IAM, task definitions)
- ALLOW service teams to own their application Terraform modules — they define their service's resources
- REQUIRE service teams to consume platform outputs via interfaces — they do not reach into platform state
- USE a platform team to maintain shared infrastructure — clear ownership prevents platform drift
- PROVIDE a service template/scaffold module that encodes platform standards (tagging, security groups, IAM baseline)

Trade-offs:
- Per-service modules: independent deployments, clear ownership vs. proliferation of small state files to manage
- Platform/service split: clean boundaries vs. coordination required when platform changes break service contracts
- Service team autonomy: fast deployments vs. risk of diverging from platform standards without guardrails
- Shared platform: efficient resource use vs. platform team becomes a bottleneck for service teams

Anti-patterns:
- Giving service teams direct access to modify platform (VPC, EKS) infrastructure — accidental network changes affect all services
- Service teams duplicating VPC and cluster resources — costly and creates network segmentation confusion
- No platform team — platform infrastructure accumulates tech debt and drift with no clear ownership
- Service modules that reach directly into another service's state — tight coupling between service deployments

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Operational Excellence: Conway's Law alignment reduces coordination overhead between teams
- Reliability: independent deployment of services limits blast radius of infrastructure changes
- Security Pillar: service-level IAM isolation through per-service task roles and IRSA

Multi-Account AWS Strategy

Multi-account AWS architecture uses AWS Organizations to create hard isolation boundaries between environments, workloads, and business units. Account-level isolation is the strongest security and blast radius boundary available in AWS — it cannot be bypassed by IAM misconfiguration. The AWS recommended account vending structure uses a management account, shared services account (logging, security tooling), and workload accounts per environment and business domain.

Decision rules:
- USE multi-account WHEN: production security requirements mandate strict isolation, compliance (PCI, HIPAA, SOC 2) is required, or organization > 20 engineers
- MINIMUM viable multi-account: management account (billing, Organizations), log archive account, security tooling account, prod workload account, non-prod workload account
- CENTRALIZE CloudTrail logs and GuardDuty in a dedicated log archive account — prevents tampering by individual workload accounts
- USE AWS Control Tower for new multi-account setups — automates baseline guardrails, log aggregation, and account vending
- USE AWS Transit Gateway for cross-account VPC connectivity — hub-and-spoke routing over individual VPC peering at scale
- PROVISION accounts with Terraform via aws_organizations_account resource and account-level Terraform modules
- DEFINE Service Control Policies to enforce: MFA requirement, region restriction, prohibited service usage (e.g., no root account usage)

Trade-offs:
- Multi-account: strongest isolation, compliance-ready vs. significant initial setup overhead, cross-account IAM complexity
- Control Tower: fast standardized setup vs. opinionated — deviating from Control Tower defaults is difficult
- Transit Gateway: scalable hub-and-spoke routing vs. hourly cost per attachment and data processing fees
- Account-per-environment vs. environment VPCs in shared account: hard isolation vs. simpler networking

Anti-patterns:
- All workloads in a single AWS account — IAM misconfiguration, runaway Lambda, or cost anomaly affects all workloads
- Manual account creation without Terraform — accounts drift from baseline immediately after creation
- No Service Control Policies — individual account admins can deviate from organization security baseline
- VPC peering mesh between many accounts — O(n²) peering relationships become unmanageable; use Transit Gateway
- Sharing IAM roles across accounts without explicit trust policies — implicit cross-account access

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: account isolation is the AWS recommended primary security boundary
- Operational Excellence: account vending automation via Terraform enables consistent baseline across accounts
- Cost Optimization: per-account cost visibility and enforcement via AWS Budgets per account

EKS Platform Pattern — Production-Grade Kubernetes Infrastructure

A production EKS platform is more than a cluster — it is a set of shared infrastructure components that platform teams maintain and service teams consume. This includes: VPC with private subnets and VPC Endpoints, EKS cluster with managed node groups, cluster add-ons (Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter, AWS Load Balancer Controller, External DNS, External Secrets Operator, metrics-server), and GitOps delivery (ArgoCD/Flux). The terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws module is the authoritative baseline.

Decision rules:
- USE terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws as the cluster foundation — it encodes production defaults (private endpoint, log types, managed add-ons)
- ENABLE private cluster endpoint for production — control plane API is not exposed to internet
- DEPLOY AWS Load Balancer Controller via Helm — enables ALB/NLB creation from Kubernetes Ingress/Service objects
- DEPLOY External DNS — automatically manages Route53 records for Kubernetes service hostnames
- DEPLOY External Secrets Operator — syncs AWS Secrets Manager secrets into Kubernetes secrets without storing values in Git
- DEPLOY Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter — Karpenter for new clusters, Cluster Autoscaler for existing
- ENABLE IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) — each workload gets a dedicated IAM role scoped to its permissions
- CONFIGURE OIDC provider for the EKS cluster — required for IRSA to function
- SEPARATE system node group (kube-system) from application node group — prevent workload eviction of system components

Trade-offs:
- Private endpoint only: strong security vs. kubectl access requires VPN or bastion host
- Public + private endpoint: developer ergonomics vs. API surface exposed to internet (mitigated by IP allowlist)
- Karpenter: superior scaling vs. more complex initial IRSA and CRD setup than Cluster Autoscaler
- Managed Node Groups: simplified lifecycle vs. cannot customize kubelet flags or use custom bootstrap scripts

Anti-patterns:
- Public EKS API endpoint without IP restrictions — Kubernetes API exposed to internet, brute-force risk
- No IRSA — all pods inherit node IAM role permissions, violating least privilege
- Not installing AWS Load Balancer Controller — falls back to deprecated in-tree controller with no ALB/NLB support
- Not configuring Pod Security Admission or OPA Gatekeeper — pods can run as root, privileged, with host network
- Single node group for all workloads — system pods compete with application pods for resources
- Not enabling EKS control plane logging (audit, api, authenticator) — no visibility into Kubernetes API activity

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: private endpoint, IRSA, and pod security policies implement defense in depth
- Reliability Pillar: multiple node groups, Karpenter, and cluster add-ons ensure workload availability
- Operational Excellence: GitOps delivery and managed add-ons reduce cluster operational overhead

Serverless Infrastructure Pattern — Lambda + API Gateway + DynamoDB

The serverless infrastructure pattern eliminates EC2/container management entirely. AWS Lambda executes functions on-demand, API Gateway provides the HTTP layer, DynamoDB provides single-digit millisecond storage, and S3 handles object storage. This pattern achieves zero idle cost — you pay only for actual executions. It is optimal for event-driven workloads, APIs with highly variable traffic, and teams that want to eliminate infrastructure operations entirely.

Decision rules:
- CHOOSE serverless WHEN: event-driven workloads (S3 events, SNS, SQS triggers), APIs with spiky or unpredictable traffic, startup or MVP with minimal operational capacity
- CHOOSE serverless WHEN: function execution time < 15 minutes and function is stateless
- USE Lambda provisioned concurrency for latency-sensitive functions — eliminates cold starts at cost of pre-warmed instances
- USE DynamoDB on-demand capacity for new serverless applications — scales to zero, no capacity planning
- USE DynamoDB provisioned + Auto Scaling when read/write pattern is predictable — 30-50% cheaper than on-demand
- USE SQS + Lambda for decoupled asynchronous processing — natural backpressure and retry behavior
- USE Step Functions for complex multi-step serverless workflows — visual debugging, built-in error handling

Trade-offs:
- Lambda: zero idle cost vs. cold starts add 100-3000ms latency for first request per container
- Serverless: no infrastructure management vs. distributed tracing and debugging is harder
- DynamoDB on-demand: zero capacity planning vs. 6-7x more expensive than provisioned for steady traffic
- Lambda: infinite concurrency by default vs. can accidentally DDoS downstream services (set reserved concurrency)

Anti-patterns:
- Running long-running jobs on Lambda — 15-minute timeout kills incomplete operations, use ECS Fargate instead
- Lambda with synchronous chains longer than 3 hops — cumulative latency degrades UX and complicates debugging
- No DLQ (Dead Letter Queue) on Lambda — failed invocations are silently lost
- Not setting Lambda reserved concurrency — function can consume entire account concurrency limit (1000 default)
- Using Lambda for CPU-intensive tasks (video encoding, ML inference) — EC2 or SageMaker are more cost-effective
- Monolith Lambda (one function handles all routes) — loses independent deployability and cold start isolation

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Cost Optimization: pay-per-execution eliminates idle infrastructure cost completely
- Operational Excellence: no server management reduces undifferentiated operational work
- Reliability Pillar: Lambda's built-in AZ-level redundancy and automatic retry on async invocations

Hub-and-Spoke Networking Pattern — Transit Gateway

Hub-and-spoke networking uses AWS Transit Gateway as a central routing hub connecting multiple VPCs (spokes) across accounts and regions. This replaces a mesh of VPC peering connections that becomes unmanageable beyond 5-10 VPCs. Transit Gateway enables centralized network security inspection, route table management, and consistent connectivity policies. It is required for multi-account architectures with >5 VPCs.

Decision rules:
- USE Transit Gateway WHEN: > 5 VPCs need connectivity, multi-account architecture, or centralized network inspection required
- USE VPC Peering WHEN: ≤ 3 VPCs with simple connectivity requirements — lower cost and complexity
- ATTACH a network security VPC (inspection VPC with AWS Network Firewall or third-party appliance) to Transit Gateway for egress inspection
- CONFIGURE Transit Gateway route tables to segment traffic: dev VPCs cannot route to prod VPCs directly
- SHARE Transit Gateway across accounts via AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) — one TGW per region serves all accounts
- PLAN Transit Gateway CIDR carefully — VPC CIDRs across all attached VPCs must not overlap

Trade-offs:
- Transit Gateway: scalable, centrally managed vs. $0.05/GB data processing + $0.07/hour per attachment
- VPC Peering: free data transfer within AZ vs. O(n²) connections become unmanageable
- Centralized inspection: consistent security policy vs. all traffic traverses inspection VPC (latency and cost)
- Full mesh vs. hub-spoke: lower latency vs. unmanageable at scale

Anti-patterns:
- VPC peering mesh for >10 VPCs — each new VPC requires n-1 new peering connections
- Not segmenting Transit Gateway route tables — dev and prod VPCs can route to each other without restriction
- Overlapping CIDRs across VPCs attached to the same Transit Gateway — routing becomes ambiguous or broken
- Not using RAM to share Transit Gateway — creates redundant TGWs per account, multiplying cost

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Security Pillar: centralized inspection VPC enforces consistent egress and east-west traffic policies
- Operational Excellence: single TGW per region simplifies network topology for operations teams
- Reliability: Transit Gateway multi-AZ and multi-region routing provides network-level fault tolerance

Infrastructure as Code Maturity Model

IaC maturity is not binary — organizations progress through stages from manual provisioning to fully automated, policy-driven infrastructure. Understanding the maturity model allows an AI agent to recommend the correct level of automation complexity for the organization's current state, rather than recommending advanced patterns to teams that will fail to maintain them.

Decision rules:
- STAGE 1 — Getting Started: single root module, local or S3 state, manual apply, one environment. Appropriate for: proof of concept, single engineer
- STAGE 2 — Structured: separate modules per component, remote state with locking, environments via directories, pipeline for apply. Appropriate for: small teams (2-5 engineers), single application
- STAGE 3 — Standardized: module library, policy scanning (tfsec/Checkov), tagging enforcement, secrets in Secrets Manager, multi-environment pipelines. Appropriate for: growing teams, production-critical workloads
- STAGE 4 — Platform: self-service infrastructure, internal module registry, automated account vending, drift detection, cost allocation dashboards. Appropriate for: platform teams, 10+ engineering teams
- RECOMMEND the current stage's practices, not aspirational — teams at Stage 1 should not implement Stage 4 tooling
- PRIORITIZE removing manual toil at each stage before advancing — automate the most painful process first

Trade-offs:
- Higher maturity: more automation, less toil vs. higher upfront investment and tooling complexity
- Advancing too fast: technical debt from immature practices vs. overwhelming teams with too many tools simultaneously
- Platform investment: enables other teams vs. platform team is a cost center until critical mass

Anti-patterns:
- Implementing Terraform Enterprise/Cloud for a 2-person team — enterprise tooling costs exceed the team's value from it
- Skipping Stage 2 fundamentals (remote state, module structure) and jumping to Stage 4 tooling
- Treating IaC maturity as complete — infrastructure automation is a continuous improvement discipline
- Platform team building self-service tools before anyone uses the platform manually — automate observed pain, not imagined pain

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Operational Excellence: the maturity model aligns with AWS's guidance on operational capability building
- Cost Optimization: each maturity stage adds visibility and control that reduces infrastructure waste

Application Profile to Infrastructure Mapping — Decision Framework

An application profile describes the workload characteristics that drive infrastructure decisions. The AI infrastructure agent must translate profile attributes into infrastructure choices. This entry codifies the mapping rules that a senior architect uses to move from 'application description' to 'infrastructure recommendation'. It integrates all previous patterns into a unified decision tree.

Decision rules:
- IF traffic_pattern = spiky OR event_driven AND execution_time < 15min → recommend Lambda + API Gateway
- IF traffic_pattern = steady AND team_kubernetes_maturity = low AND services < 10 → recommend ECS Fargate
- IF traffic_pattern = steady AND team_kubernetes_maturity = high OR services > 10 → recommend EKS
- IF workload = batch_processing AND duration < 15min → recommend Lambda + SQS
- IF workload = batch_processing AND duration > 15min → recommend ECS Fargate + SQS or AWS Batch
- IF data_model = relational AND scale = moderate → recommend RDS PostgreSQL/MySQL Multi-AZ
- IF data_model = relational AND scale = high AND workload = variable → recommend Aurora Serverless v2
- IF data_model = key_value OR document AND scale = high AND latency = single_digit_ms → recommend DynamoDB
- IF team_size < 5 AND stage = early → recommend single-account, single-region, monolith infrastructure
- IF team_size > 20 OR compliance_required = true → recommend multi-account AWS Organizations
- IF availability_requirement = 99.99% → require 3-AZ deployment, Multi-AZ RDS, ALB, Auto Scaling
- IF security_sensitivity = high (PCI, HIPAA) → require private subnets, VPC Endpoints, private EKS endpoint, Secrets Manager, CloudTrail, GuardDuty

Trade-offs:
- Lambda-first: zero infrastructure vs. cold start latency and 15-min limit constraint
- EKS-first: maximum flexibility vs. highest operational overhead — only justified at scale
- Multi-account early: best isolation vs. operational overhead before team has scale to manage it
- Aurora Serverless: variable cost vs. cold start for infrequently accessed databases

Anti-patterns:
- Recommending EKS to every application regardless of scale — Kubernetes is a platform, not a default
- Recommending Lambda for CPU-bound or stateful workloads — fundamental mismatch
- Recommending single-AZ for any production workload — availability requirement eliminates single-AZ
- Recommending RDS single-AZ for databases with RPO < 1 hour
- Ignoring team maturity in infrastructure recommendations — the best architecture for the wrong team creates operational risk

AWS Well-Architected alignment:
- Performance Efficiency: matching infrastructure to workload characteristics is the core Performance Efficiency pillar practice
- Cost Optimization: right-fit infrastructure avoids over/under-provisioning penalties
- Reliability: matching HA architecture to availability requirements without gold-plating low-criticality workloads
